subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffee Reaches the Americas
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Coffee Reaches the Americas.

hook.text: In 1714, the Mayor of Amsterdam gave King Louis XIV a single coffee plant. It changed the world.

buildup.text: A French naval officer named Gabriel de Clieu stole a cutting from the royal greenhouse in Paris.

discovery.text: De Clieu sailed to Martinique in 1723, sharing his water ration with the plant during a drought at sea.

twist.text: That single plant produced 18,680 coffee trees within 50 years. Nearly all Caribbean coffee descends from it.

climax.text: From Martinique, coffee spread to Central and South America—the region now produces 60% of the world's coffee.

punchline.text: One stolen cutting. Billions of cups. Every single day.

quiz.question: How did coffee reach the Caribbean?
options: A French officer smuggled a cutting to Martinique

details.summary: Coffee arrived in the Americas in the early 1700s through a remarkable chain of events. A French naval officer, Gabriel de Clieu, reportedly shared his water ration with a single coffee plant during a perilous voyage to Martinique. From that Caribbean start, coffee spread across Latin America.
details.whyItMatters: The introduction of coffee to the Americas set the stage for the continent to become the world's dominant producing region, reshaping economies from Brazil to Colombia.
takeaways: Gabriel de Clieu brought coffee to Martinique around 1720
From the Caribbean, coffee spread throughout Latin America
The Americas became the world's dominant coffee-producing region

faq.question: Is the story of Gabriel de Clieu true?
faq.answer: De Clieu wrote about the voyage himself, describing pirate attacks, storms, and sharing his water with the plant. While likely embellished, records confirm he did bring coffee to Martinique around 1720. Within decades, coffee had spread to most French and Spanish Caribbean colonies.

faq.question: How did coffee spread from the Caribbean to mainland Americas?
faq.answer: Seeds and cuttings from Caribbean plantations spread quickly. The Dutch brought coffee to Suriname, the Portuguese to Brazil, and the Spanish to Central America. By the late 1700s, coffee was grown across Latin America. Brazil's explosion in the 1800s made it the world's dominant producer.
